title: Telling the time, and naming the day
goal: Ask and give the time, name the days and months, say a date, and handle the words that carve up an Indonesian day — which starts earlier and divides differently than yours.
bekal: ask *Jam berapa?* and answer to the half hour and the quarter hour
name any day, month and date
arrange to meet someone at a specific time on a specific day

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bikin janji
dialogs.intro: Rina and Sarah are trying to find a time to visit a batik exhibition.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.id: Sarah, are you busy on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sabtu pagi ada les bahasa. Siang kosong.
lines.id: Saturday morning I have a language class. The afternoon is free.
lines.literal: Saturday morning exist lesson language. midday empty.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Bagus. Ada pameran batik di Museum Tekstil.
lines.id: Good. There's a batik exhibition at the Textile Museum.
lines.literal: good. exist exhibition batik at Museum Textile.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Interesting! What time does it open?

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Jam sembilan sampai jam empat sore.
lines.id: Nine until four in the afternoon.
lines.literal: hour nine until hour four afternoon.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Jam satu siang di depan museum. Bisa?
lines.id: One o'clock in front of the museum. Can you?
lines.literal: hour one midday at front museum. can?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Bisa. Tapi les saya selesai jam dua belas.
lines.id: Yes. But my class finishes at twelve.
lines.literal: can. but lesson I finish hour twelve.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Kalau begitu jam setengah dua saja.
lines.id: In that case let's say half past one.
lines.literal: if like-that hour half two only.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Setengah dua? Jam satu tiga puluh, ya?
lines.literal: half two? hour one three ten, yes?

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Betul. Setengah jalan menuju jam dua.
lines.literal: correct. half road heading hour two.

notes: **Setengah dua means half past ONE.** This is the single most dangerous piece of A1 Indonesian for an English speaker. *Setengah* is "half", and the number after it is the hour you are heading **towards** — the German and Dutch system. *Setengah dua* = halfway to two = 1.30. Get this wrong once and you will be an hour early, which in Indonesia at least is the better mistake.
**Jam does two jobs**: "hour", "o'clock", and also "clock/watch". *Jam berapa?* is "what time is it?", *jam satu* is "one o'clock", and *jam saya* is "my watch".

**Hari Sabtu, not just Sabtu.** In careful Indonesian the word *hari* ("day") goes in front of the day's name: *hari Senin*, *hari Sabtu*. In speech it is often dropped, but including it is never wrong.

**Ketemu is the everyday form of bertemu.** Both mean "to meet"; *bertemu* is the written one you met in Unit 1, *ketemu* is what people say. You will find this pattern again and again — the spoken form is shorter.
**Kalau begitu — "in that case".** *Kalau* is "if", *begitu* is "like that". This phrase is the hinge of countless conversations and is worth memorising whole.

grammars.title: The clock
body: Indonesian counts hours from one to twelve and adds a part of the day when it matters.
after: 💬 In practice, most people now simply read the digits: *jam satu tiga puluh* or *jam tujuh belas* (17.00), especially for appointments and timetables. If you find *setengah dua* too dangerous to produce, say *jam satu tiga puluh* — it is perfectly normal Indonesian, and unambiguous.
*Lewat* ("past") and *kurang* ("less") do the same work as in English. *Seperempat* is "a quarter" — there is that *se-* meaning "one" again.

grammars.title: The parts of an Indonesian day
body: The day is divided differently from English, and the divisions are used constantly with times.
after: Indonesia sits on the equator, so sunrise and sunset barely move all year: roughly six in the morning and six in the evening, every day, everywhere in the country. That is why these divisions are so stable — and why *sore* is a real, distinct part of the day rather than a vague "late afternoon".
The country has three time zones: **WIB** (Jakarta, Sumatra, Java), **WITA** (Bali, Kalimantan, Sulawesi) and **WIT** (Papua), each an hour apart. Flight times and TV listings always say which.

blocks.text: Dates run **day, month, year**, with no ordinal ending: *tanggal 17 Agustus 1945* — the seventeenth of August 1945, Indonesian independence day, and a date every Indonesian knows. Ask with *Tanggal berapa?* ("what date?") and *Hari apa?* ("what day?").
⚠️ *Minggu* with a capital M is Sunday; *minggu* with a small one is a week. *Minggu depan* is "next week", *hari Minggu* is "Sunday". Speech makes no distinction, so the sentence has to.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: Sorry, I already have an appointment.

blocks.text: 💬 You may hear the phrase *jam karet* — "rubber time" — used with a shrug when someone arrives half an hour late. It is a real and self-aware part of Indonesian social life. Business and formal appointments, however, are expected to start on time, and being punctual will never count against you.

items: Let's meet at half past one.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
